newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's Fin Min proposes price stability target.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Fin Min proposes price stability target.

text.p: Sweden's Finance Ministry proposed on Tuesday that price stability should remain the main central bank target as part of a broader move to improve confidence in monetary and foreign exchange policies.
However, the finance ministry said the Riksbank should also support general economic trends without jeopardizing this goal.
"For the past several years, the primary objective of the Riksbank has been to maintain price stability," the Finance Ministry said in a statement.
"This will remain as the primary objective for monetary policy and will now be established by law," it said.
"In addition, without prejudice to the objective of price stability, the Riksbank shall support general economic policy with the purpose of promoting long-term growth and a high level of employment."
The latter does not need to be regulated by law because the economic policy objectives formulated by parliament must be regarded as guidelines for the Riksbank, the ministry said.

The string of measures are based on a five-party agreement and are either related to Sweden's obligations as a member of the European Union (EU) or have been raised by the Commission responsible for foreign exchange policies, the ministry said.
The ministry also proposed a new rule, prohibiting all authorities to give instructions to the Riksbank on matters pertaining to monetary policy.
"In addition, the Act on the Riksbank will forbid high ranking civil servants of the bank to seek or take instruction from anyone," it said.
The Riksbank governor will also obtain a stronger position.
"The governor may be relieved from office only if he no longer fulfils the conditions required for the performance of his duties or if he has been guilty of serious misconduct," the ministry said.
The Riksbank will also have to inform the finance minister before all important monetary and foreign exchange decisions are made, the ministry said.
All these measures are in line with phase two of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) which Sweden is bound to carry out as a member of the EU, the ministry said.
"The agreement, however, does not mean that a position has been taken on whether Sweden should or should not join the European Monetary Union," Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said.
"The measures are of such a nature that they must be carried out regardless of the decision on the EMU issue," he said.

As the EU Treaty lays down strong conflict of interest rules for those who make monetary policy decisions, the finance ministry proposed a new management structure for the Riksbank, resembling that of many other central banks.
"The new Governing Board will not have any responsibility for monetary policy," the ministry said. "Instead it will have more of a supervisory role of the (new) Directorate."
The Board will appoint the members of the Directorate with parliament appointing Board delegates.

"The Directorate shall be the Riksbank's operating management with the primary responsibility of independently making all monetary decisions," the ministry said, adding that the Riksbank governor should be chairman of the Directorate.
The Board's chairman and vice chairman will have the right to attend and speak at the Directorate's meeting in a non-voting capacity, it said.
The government will take over decisions regarding foreign exchange systems, the ministry said.
"In line with what is applied in other member states of the European Union, the government shall determine the foreign exchange system in the future," the Ministry said.
"The Riksbank shall determine the central rate and fluctuation margins in a system with a fixed exchange rate and manage a floating exchange rate regime."

The five parties agreeing on these measures encompass the ruling Social Democrats, its informal cooperation partner the Centre Party, the Liberal Party, the Christian Democrats and the conservative Moderate Party.
"The agreement will strengthen the Riksbank's independence and will increase the confidence in Swedish monetary and foreign exchange policies," Asbrink said.
-- Birgitta Forsberg, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017
